title: The Birth of Samson Announced
summary: Israel does evil again and falls under Philistine rule for forty years. The angel of the LORD appears to the barren wife of Manoah, a Danite, promising a son who will be a Nazirite from the womb and will begin to deliver Israel. Manoah asks for a second visit, offers a sacrifice, and sees the angel ascend in the flame; Samson is born, grows, and the Spirit of the LORD begins to stir him.
story: This is the last cycle of a judge in the book, and it opens with the familiar formula of Israel's evil and God's handing them over. But something is missing: for the first time, Israel doesn't cry out to the LORD. The people seem to have accepted Philistine rule, and the deliverance begins from God's side alone, with a birth announcement to a childless woman. The previous judges were called as adults; Samson is set apart before he is conceived. The chapter raises high hopes, for a child dedicated to God, announced by a heavenly messenger, and given the Spirit. Chapters 14-16 will show how far Samson falls short of those hopes, and how God still works through him.
historical:
The Philistines were among the Sea Peoples, groups from the Aegean and eastern Mediterranean who moved into the coastal lands of the Levant around 1200 BC, at the end of the Late Bronze Age. Egyptian records from the reign of Ramesses III, including temple reliefs at Medinet Habu, describe battles with these peoples and name one group the Peleset, generally identified with the Philistines. They settled on the southern coastal plain of Canaan in five main cities, Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, and Gath (Joshua 13:3), each ruled by a lord. Excavations at these sites show a distinct material culture, including decorated pottery with Aegean roots.

The Philistines were technologically and militarily strong, and they pressed east into the lowland hills (the Shephelah) where the tribe of Dan had been allotted land (Joshua 19:40-48). Zorah and Eshtaol, Manoah's home region, lay in the Sorek Valley on this frontier. The forty years of Philistine domination connect with the opening of 1 Samuel, where Philistine pressure continues into Samuel's time.
cultural:
Barrenness in the ancient Near East brought grief and often shame, since children secured a family's name, labor, inheritance, and care in old age. In Scripture, a series of barren women receive children by God's intervention: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah, and later Elizabeth. Each time the child plays a decisive role, and the birth itself signals that God is acting.

The Nazirite vow is described in Numbers 6. Normally it was a temporary vow taken by an adult man or woman, who for a set time abstained from wine and anything from the grapevine, let the hair grow uncut, and avoided contact with a dead body. Samson's case is unusual in three ways: the vow is imposed by God, it begins before birth (so his mother must keep the food restrictions during pregnancy), and it lasts for life. Samuel is also dedicated from birth with a promise that no razor will touch his head (1 Samuel 1:11). Manoah's offer of a meal to the visitor follows the custom of hospitality seen with Abraham in Genesis 18, and his fear on realizing whom he has seen reflects a common belief, grounded in Exodus 33:20, that no one could see God and live.
literary: The chapter is shaped by repetition and by a quiet contrast between husband and wife. The angel's instructions are given three times (13:3-5, 13:7 in the woman's report, and 13:13-14), with small variations: when the woman retells them, she adds that the boy will be a Nazirite until the day of his death, a detail that hangs over the whole Samson story. Manoah is anxious and a step behind. He asks for the messenger to return, but the messenger comes back to his wife; he asks questions the angel has already answered; he wants to feed the visitor and learn his name. His wife, never named, understands more. When Manoah panics that they will die, she reasons calmly that God would not have accepted their offering and told them these things if he meant to kill them. The scene of the angel rising in the flame is the chapter's climax, and it echoes Gideon's encounter in 6:19-22.

outline.t: Israel's evil and forty years under the Philistines
The angel of the LORD appears to Manoah's wife
Manoah prays, and the angel returns
The offering, the hidden name, and the angel in the flame
Samson is born, blessed, and stirred by the Spirit

doctrines.note: Israel does not even cry out, yet God begins a deliverance. The initiative is entirely his, from the announcement to the birth, which shows grace preceding any request.
The Nazirite vow sets Samson apart for God from the womb. Holiness in the Old Testament means belonging to God in a distinct way, marked here by visible signs in food, hair, and conduct.

The angel of the LORD speaks for God, receives no offering for himself, and has a name beyond comprehension. Manoah concludes that they have seen God, which raises the question of how God can be present in a visible messenger.

words.note: Nazir, a Nazirite, one separated or consecrated. The word comes from a root meaning to separate or dedicate. Numbers 6 gives the regulations. For Samson, the Nazirite status is the core of his identity and calling, and his hair becomes its visible sign, which is why the loss of it in chapter 16 is so serious.

Mal'akh, messenger or angel, used twelve times here. The same word can refer to human messengers (as in 11:12) or heavenly ones. The angel of the LORD in the Old Testament sometimes speaks as God himself, and interpreters differ on whether he is a created angel speaking for God or a visible appearance of God, with many Christian readers seeing an appearance of the Son before the incarnation.

Pil'i, beyond comprehension or wonderful. The angel's name is too wonderful to be grasped. The word belongs to a family (pele, wonder; pala, to do wonders, used in 13:19) that describes things only God can do. The same family appears in the name Wonderful Counselor in Isaiah 9:6.

Aqar, barren. The word is used of Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, and Hannah, placing Manoah's wife in a line of women through whom God acts at turning points. A barren womb underlines that the coming deliverer is God's gift, not a human achievement.

christ: The chapter belongs to a biblical pattern of promised births that runs to the New Testament. An angel announces a son to a woman who cannot have children, names his role in God's plan, and sets him apart from the womb. The announcement to Zechariah about John the Baptist, who will drink no wine or strong drink (Luke 1:13-17), echoes this closely, and the announcement to Mary (Luke 1:26-38) surpasses it: not a barren woman but a virgin, not a Nazirite who will begin to save Israel but the Son of God who will save his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21). Samson will only begin the deliverance from the Philistines, as the angel says in 13:5; the work will be carried on by Samuel and completed by David. The pattern points forward to a deliverer who will finish what he begins. Some Christian readers also see in the angel with the wonderful name an appearance of the Son; that is an interpretation, not something the chapter states.

hard.q: Who is the angel of the LORD, and did Manoah really see God?
hard.a: The text uses the terms the angel of the LORD, a man of God, and God almost interchangeably, and Manoah concludes that they have seen God (13:22). Similar scenes with Hagar, Abraham, Moses at the bush, and Gideon show the same pattern. Interpreters give three main answers. Many Jewish and some Christian readers understand him as a created angel who bears God's name and speaks with God's authority, so that meeting him is like meeting God. Many Christian interpreters, from the early church on, have seen him as a visible appearance of God, often identified with the Son before his incarnation. Others think the messenger is a way of describing God's own presence without claiming that God himself is visible. The chapter's point is clear on any reading: God personally initiated this birth and this deliverance, and his presence is both gracious and overwhelming.

questions: Israel did not cry out for help this time, yet God began to deliver them anyway. What does that show about the source of rescue?
Manoah's wife understood the situation more clearly than her husband. Why do you think the narrator draws this contrast?
Samson was set apart for God before he was born. What does it mean for a calling to come before a person's own choices, and how can a person fail to live up to it?
